source_text: Superior de principiis Levitici dictum est; nunc lex sacrificiorum quae munera appellantur. Anima quae peccaverit ex populo — non voluntate semper, sed ignorantia — munus offert. Synagoga et anima typice leguntur.
thought_title: Transition from principles to the law of sacrifices
orientation: Origen has just finished the moral application of the burnt offering and now turns to the law of sacrifices, called 'gifts,' beginning with the soul that sins from ignorance.
pass_a_gloss: The previous part has been spoken about the principles of Leviticus; now the law of sacrifices which are called gifts. The soul which has sinned from the people — not always by will, but by ignorance — offers a gift. The synagogue and the soul are read typically.

choices.why: The source explicitly says the sacrifices are called munera, and the glossary reserves 'sacrifice' for sacrificium; 'gifts' preserves the distinct term.
The adverb signals figural reading, matching the glossary's 'figure' for figura; 'typically' keeps the technical sense of type.
The relative clause with perfect subjunctive is rendered as a generalizing relative clause, preserving the indefinite force.

choices.english: not always by will, but by ignorance
choices.why: The ablatives of manner are kept as prepositional phrases; 'always' modifies the whole contrast, matching the Latin word order.
rejected: not by will always, but by ignorance

pass_b_english: We have spoken already about the principles of Leviticus; now we come to the law of the sacrifices that are called gifts. The soul which has sinned from among the people—not always by will, but by ignorance—offers a gift. The synagogue and the soul are read as figures.

last_rejected.quote: not always by will, but by ignorance
last_rejected.why: Latin 'semper' modifies 'voluntate', meaning 'not by will always' i.e. not always voluntary; English inverts to 'not always by will', changing scope of 'always'.
last_rejected.fix: not by will always, but by ignorance
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'non voluntate semper' and English 'not always by will' express same scope: sin is not always voluntary. No meaning change.
